To find the resultant voltage $V(t) = V_1(t) + V_2(t)$, we can use the phasor addition method.

Given voltages:
$$V_1(t) = 30\sin(\omega t + 45^\circ) \implies \mathbf{V}_1 = 30 \angle 45^\circ$$
$$V_2(t) = 60\sin(\omega t + 60^\circ) \implies \mathbf{V}_2 = 60 \angle 60^\circ$$

Convert each phasor into its rectangular form ($x + jy$):
$$\mathbf{V}_1 = 30(\cos 45^\circ + j\sin 45^\circ) = 30(0.7071 + j0.7071) = 21.21 + j21.21$$
$$\mathbf{V}_2 = 60(\cos 60^\circ + j\sin 60^\circ) = 60(0.5 + j0.866) = 30 + j51.96$$

Add the real and imaginary parts:
$$\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}_1 + \mathbf{V}_2 = (21.21 + 30) + j(21.21 + 51.96) = 51.21 + j73.17$$

Convert the resultant phasor back to polar form (magnitude $V_m$ and phase angle $\phi$):
$$V_m = \sqrt{(51.21)^2 + (73.17)^2} = \sqrt{2622.46 + 5353.85} = \sqrt{7976.31} = 89.31$$
$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{73.17}{51.21}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1.4288) = 55.01^\circ$$

Thus, the resultant voltage in the required form is:
$$V(t) = 89.31\sin(\omega t + 55.01^\circ)$$
proTip: Always convert sinusoidal equations into their corresponding polar phasor forms before adding or subtracting them.
